ru: отрекаться от престола, отречься; слагать с себя (обязанности)
transitivity: both — transitive (*he abdicated the throne*), intransitive (*the king abdicated in 1936*)
gloss: To give up a throne, a position of power, or a responsibility that belongs to you.
examples: A monarch may *abdicate* in favor of a younger heir.
Edward VIII *abdicated* in order to marry an American.
Critics say the agency has *abdicated* its duty to protect consumers.

gloss: To help or encourage someone to do something wrong, especially a crime.
examples: Anyone who helps *abet* a fraud can be charged too.
He *abetted* the robbery by driving the getaway car.
She was convicted of aiding and *abetting* the escape.
contrast: The final *t* doubles: *abetted, abetting*. In American legal English it almost always appears in the pair *aid and abet*.

gloss: To hate something very strongly, usually because you think it is morally wrong.
examples: I *abhor* cruelty of any kind.
She *abhorred* the idea of asking her family for money.
He has always *abhorred* violence, even in self-defense.
contrast: The final *r* doubles: *abhorred, abhorring*. Like *hate*, it is a state verb, so the continuous (*I am abhorring*) sounds wrong.

gloss: To exist in very large numbers or quantities.
examples: Rumors *abound* about who will get the job.
Wildflowers *abounded* on the hillside that spring.
Theories have *abounded* ever since the story broke.
contrast: To name what is plentiful, use *abound with* or *abound in*: *the lake abounds with fish*.

gloss: To wear away or scrape a surface by rubbing against it.
examples: Wind and sand slowly *abrade* the sandstone.
The rope *abraded* his palms before he let go.
The paint had been *abraded* by years of weather.
contrast: The related words are *abrasion* (the injury) and *abrasive* (the adjective).

gloss: To cancel a law, treaty, or agreement by official action.
examples: No president can *abrogate* a treaty on his own, the senators argued.
The new government *abrogated* the agreement within a month.
Several clauses have quietly been *abrogated* since then.

ru: скрываться, сбегать (с деньгами); скрыться от правосудия
gloss: To leave quickly and secretly, usually after stealing something or to avoid arrest.
examples: If the suspects *abscond*, the bank loses the money for good.
The treasurer *absconded* with nearly a million dollars.
Two defendants have *absconded* while out on bail.
contrast: You *abscond with* money and *abscond from* a place.

transitivity: both — transitive (*their yard abuts the highway*), intransitive (*their yard abuts on the highway*)
gloss: To touch something along one side, or to share a border with it.
examples: Their property *abuts* the national forest.
The new wing *abutted* the old library wall.
Houses *abutting* the freeway get the worst of the noise.
contrast: The final *t* doubles: *abutted, abutting*.

gloss: To make one part of something stand out, or to stress a syllable or word.
examples: Designers often *accent* a plain room with one bright color.
She *accented* the wrong syllable and everyone smiled.
The dish is *accented* with lemon and fresh mint.
contrast: *Accent* is the everyday word for emphasizing a detail; *accentuate* is its more formal cousin.

transitivity: both — intransitive (*climbers acclimatize slowly*), transitive (*they acclimatized the plants first*)
gloss: To get used to a new climate, altitude, or set of conditions, or to help someone do so.
examples: Climbers need a week to *acclimatize* before the summit push.
We *acclimatized* to the heat after a few days.
The seedlings are still *acclimatizing* to life outdoors.
contrast: Americans more often say the shorter *acclimate*; British English spells this verb *acclimatise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the law accords them equal rights*), intransitive (*his story accords with the video*)
gloss: To formally give someone a right, an honor, or a kind of treatment, or to agree with something.
examples: The statute *accords* refugees the same protections as citizens.
The city *accorded* the astronaut a hero's welcome.
His account does not *accord* with what the cameras recorded.
contrast: In the intransitive sense it takes *with*. The fixed phrases are *in accordance with* and *of one's own accord*.

ru: приставать (к прохожему), подходить с разговором; окликнуть
gloss: To go up to a stranger and speak to them in a bold or threatening way.
examples: Panhandlers sometimes *accost* tourists outside the station.
A reporter *accosted* him as he left the courthouse.
She was *accosted* by two men in the parking garage.

gloss: To make yourself or someone else get used to something.
examples: It takes a few minutes to *accustom* your eyes to the dark.
He *accustomed* himself to getting up at five.
We are not *accustomed* to this kind of cold.
contrast: It takes *to* plus a noun or an *-ing* form: *accustomed to waiting*, never "accustomed to wait".

transitivity: both — transitive (*the kitchen adjoins the porch*), intransitive (*the two lots adjoin*)
gloss: To be next to something and touching it.
examples: The two offices *adjoin* each other.
A small garden *adjoined* the kitchen.
They booked *adjoining* rooms at the hotel.
contrast: Do not mix up *adjoin* (to be next to) with *adjourn* (to end a meeting): *the rooms adjoin*, but *the court adjourns*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*a judge will adjudicate the claim*), intransitive (*the panel adjudicates on appeals*)
gloss: To make an official decision about a dispute or a claim.
examples: A federal judge will *adjudicate* the dispute next month.
The board *adjudicated* more than two hundred claims last year.
The case is still being *adjudicated*.

gloss: To make a food, drink, or drug impure or weaker by adding something cheaper to it.
examples: Some sellers *adulterate* honey with cheap corn syrup.
Inspectors found that the milk had been *adulterated* with water.
The company was fined for *adulterating* its olive oil.
contrast: *Adulterate* is about mixing something impure into a product; *commit adultery* is about an unfaithful marriage. The two are not interchangeable.

gloss: To let air into something such as soil, water, or wine.
examples: You should *aerate* the lawn in early fall.
He *aerated* the wine by pouring it into a decanter.
The tank is *aerated* by a small electric pump.

gloss: To have an effect on someone or something, or to move someone emotionally.
examples: Rising interest rates *affect* everyone with a mortgage.
The storm *affected* flights all along the coast.
She was deeply *affected* by the news of his death.
contrast: *Affect* is the verb, *effect* the noun: *the storm affected flights*, but *the storm had an effect on flights*. (*Effect* as a verb exists — *effect change* — but it is formal and rare.)

ru: присоединяться, вступать в объединение; быть связанным (с организацией)
transitivity: both — intransitive (*the clinic affiliated with a hospital*), transitive (*they affiliated the school with the university*)
gloss: To join or connect formally with a larger organization.
examples: Many small clinics *affiliate* with a teaching hospital.
The union *affiliated* with a national federation in 2019.
She is *affiliated* with three research centers.
contrast: The verb ends in *-ayt* (uh-FIL-ee-ayt); the noun and adjective end in *-ut* (uh-FIL-ee-ut): *a local affiliate*.

gloss: To attach or stick something firmly onto a surface.
examples: Please *affix* a stamp to the upper right corner.
He *affixed* his signature to the contract.
A warning label had been *affixed* to the box.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (uh-FIKS); the grammar noun *affix*, meaning a prefix or suffix, is AF-iks. Third person adds *-es*: *affixes*.

gloss: To cause someone or something to suffer, especially from an illness or a lasting problem.
examples: Droughts *afflict* the region almost every summer.
A rare disease *afflicted* both brothers.
The city is *afflicted* by a chronic housing shortage.
contrast: A problem *afflicts* a person, but a person *inflicts* a problem on someone: *arthritis afflicted her*; *he inflicted pain on them*.

gloss: To make someone or something look greater or more important than they really are.
examples: Politicians rarely miss a chance to *aggrandize* themselves.
He *aggrandized* his part in the rescue with every retelling.
The legend has been *aggrandized* over the years.
contrast: The common form is the compound *self-aggrandizing*; British English spells the verb *aggrandise*.

gloss: To gather separate items or figures together into a single group or total.
examples: The site *aggregates* headlines from a hundred newspapers.
We *aggregated* three years of sales data.
Scores are *aggregated* at the end of the season.
contrast: The verb ends in *-gayt* (AG-ri-gayt); the noun and adjective end in *-guht* (AG-ri-guht), as in *in the aggregate*.

gloss: To treat someone unfairly, so that they have a real reason to complain.
examples: A ruling like this is bound to *aggrieve* somebody.
He felt deeply *aggrieved* at being passed over for the job.
The *aggrieved* party has thirty days to appeal.
contrast: You will meet it mostly as the participle *aggrieved*, which acts like an adjective: *the aggrieved employees*.

transitivity: both — intransitive (*students agitated for lower fees*), transitive (*the noise agitated the dogs*)
gloss: To campaign noisily for a change, or to make someone upset and restless.
examples: Workers began to *agitate* for shorter hours.
The long wait *agitated* the patients.
He gets *agitated* whenever the subject comes up.
contrast: In the campaigning sense it takes *for* or *against*: *agitate for reform*, *agitate against the tax*.

gloss: To worry about a decision for a long time in a painful, drawn-out way.
examples: Don't *agonize* over it — just pick one.
She *agonized* for weeks before saying no.
He has been *agonizing* about whether to sell the house.
contrast: It takes *over* or *about*. British English spells it *agonise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*what ails you?*), intransitive (*his ailing mother*)
gloss: To trouble someone or make them unwell, or to be in poor health.
examples: Tell me what *ails* you.
No one could say what *ailed* the old engine.
He spent the year caring for his *ailing* mother.
contrast: *Ail* sounds exactly like *ale*, the drink. The living form is the participle *ailing*: *an ailing economy*.

ru: транслировать, выходить в эфир; высказывать (претензии, мнение)
transitivity: both — transitive (*the network airs it on Thursdays*), intransitive (*the finale airs tonight*)
gloss: To broadcast a program, or to state an opinion or complaint publicly.
examples: The new season *airs* Thursday at eight.
The network *aired* the interview twice.
Both sides have *aired* their grievances in public.
contrast: *Air out* (a room) is a separate phrasal verb about fresh air; plain *air* is about broadcasting or speaking out.

gloss: To retouch a picture with an airbrush, or to remove awkward details from a record.
examples: Magazines still *airbrush* their cover photos.
The scar had been *airbrushed* out of the portrait.
He accused the museum of *airbrushing* him out of its own history.
contrast: Because it ends in *-sh*, the third person adds *-es*: *airbrushes*.

ru: сбрасывать с самолёта (груз, десант); сбросить на парашютах
gloss: To drop supplies or troops from an aircraft, usually by parachute.
examples: Planes will *airdrop* food into the cut-off valley.
The army *airdropped* medical supplies overnight.
Aid is being *airdropped* to villages the flood has isolated.
contrast: The final *p* doubles: *airdropped, airdropping*.

gloss: To carry people or goods by aircraft, especially in an emergency.
examples: Helicopters *airlift* injured climbers off the mountain every summer.
Rescuers *airlifted* the driver to a trauma center.
Two hundred tons of supplies have been *airlifted* in.

gloss: To make someone's fear, doubt, or anger less strong.
examples: The mayor tried to *allay* fears about the water supply.
His calm answers *allayed* most of the criticism.
Nothing the company has said has *allayed* investors' doubts.
contrast: The *y* stays because a vowel comes before it: *allayed*, not "allaid". Its usual objects are *fears, concerns, doubts, suspicions*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*they amalgamated the three offices*), intransitive (*the two banks amalgamated*)
gloss: To combine two or more organizations or things into a single one.
examples: The plan is to *amalgamate* the three departments.
Two regional banks *amalgamated* last spring.
The company was formed by *amalgamating* four small carriers.

gloss: To walk at a slow, relaxed pace.
examples: On Sundays they *amble* through the park for an hour.
He *ambled* over to the counter and ordered coffee.
We spent the morning *ambling* along the waterfront.
contrast: The silent *-e* drops before *-ing*: *ambling*.

gloss: To make a bad or painful situation better.
examples: Cash payments can *ameliorate* the worst effects of a recession.
The new rules *ameliorated* conditions in the camps.
Nothing has *ameliorated* the housing shortage so far.

gloss: To pay off a debt in regular installments, or to spread the cost of an asset over several years.
examples: Most buyers *amortize* the loan over thirty years.
The company *amortized* the software over five years.
The equipment is being *amortized* at ten percent a year.
contrast: British English spells it *amortise*.

gloss: To cut off a limb in a surgical operation.
examples: Doctors may have to *amputate* the foot.
Surgeons *amputated* his leg below the knee.
She has learned to ski since her arm was *amputated*.

gloss: To give someone a drug so that they feel no pain, usually before surgery.
examples: They will *anesthetize* the whole area before stitching it.
The vet *anesthetized* the dog for the X-ray.
The patient was fully *anesthetized* within a minute.
contrast: American English writes *anesthetize* and *anesthesia*; British English writes *anaesthetise* and *anaesthesia*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*angle the lamp toward the wall*), intransitive (*the trail angles left*)
gloss: To turn or set something at a slant.
examples: *Angle* the camera down a little.
She *angled* her chair away from the door.
He stood there *angling* the antenna until the picture cleared.
contrast: The silent *-e* drops before *-ing*: *angling*. The phrasal *angle for* (a compliment, an invitation) means to hint for something instead.

gloss: To take control of a territory and add it to your own state or city.
examples: Few governments accept any right to *annex* a neighbor's land.
Russia *annexed* Crimea in 2014.
The village was *annexed* by the city in the 1950s.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (uh-NEKS); the noun *annex*, a building added onto another, is AN-eks. Third person adds *-es*: *annexes*.

gloss: To destroy something completely, or to beat an opponent crushingly.
examples: One bad quarter could *annihilate* the company's savings.
The storm *annihilated* the entire fishing fleet.
They were *annihilated* 45–0 in the opener.
contrast: The *h* is silent: uh-NY-uh-layt.

ru: помазать (на царство), назначать преемником; умащать елеем
gloss: To put oil on someone in a religious ceremony, or to publicly choose someone as a successor.
examples: Party leaders were quick to *anoint* him as the next candidate.
The archbishop *anointed* the queen with oil.
She has been *anointed* the heir to the family business.
contrast: One *n* in the middle: *anoint*, not "annoint".

gloss: To copy someone's style or behavior, usually clumsily or without understanding it.
examples: Cheap brands *ape* the packaging of the originals.
The film *aped* Hitchcock down to the camera angles.
He got laughs by *aping* the principal's walk.
contrast: The silent *-e* drops before *-ing*: *aping*.

ru: ужасать, приводить в ужас; потрясти, шокировать
gloss: To shock someone deeply and fill them with dismay.
examples: Conditions in the shelter *appall* every visitor.
It *appalled* me that nobody called the police.
We were *appalled* by the cost of the repairs.
contrast: American English writes *appall / appalls*; British English writes *appal / appals*. Both spell the other forms *appalled* and *appalling*.

gloss: To add something at the end of a document, a list, or a file.
examples: You can *append* your comments to the report.
She *appended* a short note to the email.
A list of sources has been *appended* to the study.
contrast: You *append* something *to* a document.

gloss: To divide something up and give out the shares.
examples: The court will *apportion* the costs between the two sides.
They *apportioned* the profits equally among the partners.
Seats in the House are *apportioned* by population.

gloss: To formally inform someone of something.
examples: Please *apprise* me of any change in the schedule.
The lawyer *apprised* her client of his rights.
Staff were *apprised* of the decision by email.
contrast: *Apprise* (uh-PRYZ) means to inform; *appraise* (uh-PRAYZ) means to judge the value of something. You *apprise* someone *of* the news, but you *appraise* a house.

gloss: To take something for your own use without permission, or to set money aside officially for a purpose.
examples: Congress must *appropriate* the funds before the agency can spend them.
The label *appropriated* the design without credit or payment.
Critics say the brand has *appropriated* a sacred symbol.
contrast: Stress falls the same way, but the ending changes: the verb is uh-PROH-pree-**ayt**, while the adjective meaning "suitable" is uh-PROH-pree-**ut**.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the board approved the budget*), intransitive (*her parents did not approve*)
gloss: To officially accept a plan or request, or to think well of something.
examples: The council will *approve* the budget on Tuesday.
Regulators *approved* the drug last year.
The loan has already been *approved*.
Her parents never *approved* of the match.
contrast: Without a preposition it means to give official permission (*approve the plan*); with *of* it means to think well of something (*approve of the plan*).

ru: описывать дугу, лететь по дуге; изогнуться дугой
gloss: To move or curve along the path of an arc.
examples: Fireworks *arc* over the harbor every Fourth of July.
The ball *arced* toward the top corner of the net.
Lightning was *arcing* between the two towers.
contrast: Unlike *panic → panicked*, *arc* adds no *k* in standard American spelling: *arced, arcing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*she arched her back*), intransitive (*the bridge arches over the river*)
gloss: To bend something into a curve, or to form a curve over something.
examples: Cats *arch* their backs when they are startled.
She *arched* an eyebrow but said nothing.
Tall elms go *arching* over the whole avenue.
contrast: Because it ends in *-ch*, the third person adds *-es*: *arches*.
